'''''Tetradenia riparia''''' is a species of [[flowering plant]] native to southern Africa. It belongs in the mint and sage family [[Lamiaceae]].<ref name="CoL">{{cite web|url=http://www.catalogueoflife.org/col/details/species/id/3bab32a8747f1b0f5712a7e6d71d5d0e|title=Species Details: Tetradenia riparia (Hochst.) Codd|work=[[Catalogue of Life]]|access-date=26 January 2019}}</ref> Common names include '''ginger bush''', '''incense bush''', '''Ibozane''', and '''musk bush'''. It is occasionally referred to as '''misty plume bush''' and is commonly used as a decorative [[garden plant]] due to its flowers when in full bloom.<ref name="abc">{{Cite web|url=http://www.abc.net.au/local/stories/2010/07/12/2951352.htm|title=Passion for Plants - The Misty Plume Bush|date=12 July 2010|first=Tim|last=Entwisle|publisher=[[Australian Broadcasting Corporation]]|work=[[ABC Radio Sydney]]|access-date=26 January 2019}}</ref> 

''Tetradenia'' means 'four glands' and ''riparia'' translates to 'growing on banks of rivers'.{{citation needed|date=January 2026}}

==Description==
[[File:Tetradenia riparia 03.jpg|Inflorescence|thumb|left]]
It is a [[dioecious]], slightly [[succulent]] shrub that grows up to {{Convert|2|m|abbr=on}} high, occasionally reaching {{Convert|5|m|abbr=on}}, with irregular branch pattern. The leaves are simple, opposite, bright green, somewhat heart-shaped, sticky, aromatic, with the margin irregularly, coarsely toothed, and are {{Convert|35-80|mm|abbr=on}} long. Leaves that are crushed have a [[ginger]] scent and both sides are covered with a thin dark red lint.<ref name=pza>[https://pza.sanbi.org/tetradenia-riparia Tetradenia riparia (Hochst.)Codd] by the [[South African National Biodiversity Institute]] (SANBI). Retrieved 4 November 2024.</ref> 

The stems are brown, smooth, though younger stems feature glandular hairs and a ruby tinge, making them somewhat sticky to touch. The plant is [[deciduous]] and multi-stemmed while the branches are semi-[[succulent]].<ref name=pza/>

===Inflorescences===
The [[inflorescence]]s are [[branch]]ed, large bunches at the ends of the shoots. About three millimeters in diameter and would appear in veins, the flowers range in color from white to [[Lilac (color)|lilac]], and pink flowers are also found. Male flower spikes have more of the "mist" effect than the female flowers which tend to be more compact. Flowering occurs only in [[subtropical]] or [[temperate climate]]s in wintertime (June–August in Africa) when the plant is bare, in the top section of the branches (coinciding with the [[frost]] in the [[Highveld]] gardens).<ref>Sudhanshu Saxena, Neerja Pant, D. C. Jain et R. S. Bhakuni, « Antimalarial agents from plant sources », Current Science, novembre 2003, p. 1314-1329</ref>

==Range==
It grows on the banks of rivers and hillsides, including [[riverbank]]s, [[forest edge]]s, dry woodland valleys and hillsides where there is only minor frost. It is found in eastern [[South Africa]] in the provinces of KwaZulu-Natal, [[Mpumalanga]] and [[Limpopo]], [[Namibia]], [[Angola]] and [[Botswana]] and in eastern tropical Africa into [[Ethiopia]].<ref name=pza/>

==Cultivation==
It is commonly planted in gardens as an ornamental because of its abundant decorative flowering. Fast growing (up to 80 cm per year), the plant will flower in its first year and would prefer occasional watering in summer, though less so in winter. It prefers well drained and well composted soil, and it needs pruning after flowering. It is easily propagated by [[cuttings (plant)|cuttings]].<ref name=pza/>

===Medicinal===
This shrub is considered a [[medicinal plant]]. The [[essential oil]] of its leaves feature [[antimalarial]] contents. It is one of [[Rwanda]]'s most popular herbal remedies and has been used throughout its range to treat [[cough]], [[malaria]], [[diarrhea]], [[dengue fever]], [[headache]]s (inhaling the leaves scent), [[toothache]] and some other ailments.<ref name=pza/> 

The [[herb]] used is fresh or dried leaves and young shoots. Herbs are usually collected as needed, as they tend to black out and dry poorly. Laboratory studies have shown that the herb contains ingredients that actually moderate the malaria-causing [[Plasmodium falciparum|''Plasmodium falciparum'']] parasite. An extract from the leaves has been found to inhibit bacterial growth.<ref>SAXENA; PANT; JAIN; BHAKUNI. Antimalarial agents from plant sources. In: Current Science, v.85 n.9, nov 2003.</ref>
